questions.questionText: A designer is developing a reusable drink bottle for primary school students. Which factor should be prioritised?

choices.feedback: Correct. Materials in contact with food and the risk of small detachable parts govern this design.
Obsolescence matters over a product's life, but it does not outrank safety for a child's product.
Appearance influences uptake, but it is subordinate to safety here.
Cost constrains the solution rather than determining the priority factor.

questions.questionText: A furniture designer is selecting a finish for an outdoor bench.

criteria.description: Identifies two relevant selection criteria with justification.
Explains the environmental consequences of the chosen finish.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Identify TWO criteria the designer should apply when selecting the finish.
parts.sampleAnswer: Any two of: durability against weather and UV, safety and toxicity in an outdoor setting, ease of reapplication and maintenance, cost over the life of the bench, appearance and how it ages. One mark each, and the criterion must be justified rather than only named.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain the environmental consequences of the finish you would select.
parts.sampleAnswer: A water-based finish releases far fewer volatile organic compounds than a solvent-based one, so it is better for the applicator and for local air quality. It needs recoating more often, which uses more material over the bench's life, so the judgement should weigh the lower immediate harm against the higher ongoing use.

questions.questionText: Complete the table by naming an appropriate research method for each purpose.

rows.label: Measuring how long a task takes a user
Comparing the strength of two materials
Checking a handle is comfortable to hold

questions.questionText: Sketch a modification to the handle shown that would improve its ergonomics for a user with limited grip strength.

stimulus.alt: A cylindrical tool handle of uniform diameter
stimulus.caption: Existing handle design

config.instructions: Annotate your sketch to identify the ergonomic improvement.

markingGuide.sampleAnswer: A response worth full marks shows a larger diameter handle with a contoured or flared grip, annotated to say why: a wider grip needs less pinch force, and the flare stops the hand sliding. Marks are for the modification being ergonomically sound and clearly annotated, not for drawing quality.

criteria.description: Sketch shows a modification that plausibly reduces required grip strength.
Annotation explains why the modification helps the identified user.
Sketch is clear enough to read the intent.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the impact of emerging technologies on the work of designers, with reference to specific examples.

markingGuide.sampleAnswer: A complete response identifies emerging technologies, makes a judgement about their impact, and supports it with specific examples.

criteria.description: Makes a sustained, well-supported judgement using specific examples.
Makes a judgement with some supporting examples.
Lists relevant technologies with little development.

questions.questionText: Which factor is most affected by a designer choosing a recycled material over a virgin one?

choices.feedback: Correct. Material choice is where life cycle consequences are largely decided.
Ergonomics concerns fit to the user, which recycled content does not determine.
Recycled stock can affect appearance, but that is a consequence rather than the factor at issue.
Function is governed by performance requirements, not by the material's origin.

questions.questionText: A designer produces a scale model before manufacturing. What is its main purpose?

choices.text: To test and communicate the design before committing resources
choices.feedback: Correct. Modelling surfaces problems while changes are still cheap.

choices.text: To reduce the cost of materials
choices.feedback: A model adds cost; the saving comes from avoiding a failed production run.

choices.text: To satisfy work health and safety law
choices.feedback: Modelling is good practice, not a legal requirement.

choices.text: To replace the need for a design folio
choices.feedback: A model supports the folio rather than replacing it.

questions.questionText: Which is the clearest example of planned obsolescence?

choices.text: A device designed so its battery cannot be replaced
choices.feedback: Correct. Design that shortens usable life without a functional reason is the classic case.

choices.text: A product offered in several colours
choices.feedback: Colour choice is a marketing decision, not a life-shortening one.

choices.text: A product sold with a longer warranty
choices.feedback: A longer warranty signals the opposite intention.

choices.text: A product made from a single material for recycling
choices.feedback: Single-material construction is a design-for-recycling strategy.

questions.questionText: A designer surveys 300 people about a proposed product. This is best described as

choices.feedback: Correct. A large sample producing countable responses is quantitative.
Qualitative work explores depth with far fewer participants.
A case study examines one instance in detail.
Life cycle analysis assesses environmental impact, not opinion.

questions.questionText: Which is the strongest evidence that an innovation has succeeded commercially?

choices.text: Sustained sales and market adoption over time
choices.feedback: Correct. Commercial success is measured by adoption that lasts.
Awards recognise merit, which does not always translate to sales.
Coverage raises awareness but is not itself adoption.

choices.text: A large research and development budget
choices.feedback: Spending is an input, not evidence of a result.

questions.questionText: Anthropometric data is used by designers mainly to

choices.text: match a product's dimensions to the range of intended users
choices.feedback: Correct. Anthropometric data describes human body measurements across a population.
Costing draws on materials and process data, not body measurements.
Colour decisions are aesthetic and cultural.
Tensile testing is a materials process.

questions.questionText: A designer registers a design and applies for a patent. This protects

choices.feedback: Correct. Registration and patents are intellectual property protections.
Safety is governed by regulation and safe work practice.
Quality is managed through specification and control.
Supply chain security is a logistics concern.

choices.text: Quickly producing a physical model directly from digital data
choices.feedback: Correct. It converts digital models straight into physical parts.

choices.text: Sketching many concepts in a short time
choices.feedback: That is ideation, which is quick but not prototyping.
A production run comes after prototyping is finished.

choices.text: Surveying users about an early concept
choices.feedback: That is user research, not prototyping.

questions.questionText: A management plan for a major design project should primarily record

choices.feedback: Correct. Managing action, time and finance is what a management plan is for.
Cost alone omits sequencing and duration.
Marking criteria belong to assessment, not project management.
Inspiration belongs in the folio's research, not the plan.
